subtopics.name: The Random Nature of Radioactive Decay

parts.problem_md:
A source of water is found to be contaminated with the radioactive isotope radium-228 $( Ra_{88}^{228} )$.

This isotope of radium has a half-life of 5.75 years.

Explain the meaning of half-life in this context.
parts.solution_md:
The half-life of radium-228 is:

- The time taken for the number of atoms / nuclei / activity of radium-228; **[1 mark]**
- To be reduced to one-half (of its initial value); **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- In 5.75 years, the number of atoms / nuclei / activity of radium-228; **[1 mark]**
- Will be reduced to one-half of its current value; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A source of water is found to be contaminated with the radioactive isotope radium-228 (228/88 Ra). This isotope of radium has a half-life of 5.75 years.

Calculate the decay constant, in s<sup>–1</sup>, of radium-228.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the decay constant of radium-228:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of radium-228, $t_{1/2}$ = 5.75 years

Convert half-life into seconds:

- Half-life:  $t_{1/2}$ = 5.75 × (60 × 60 × 24 × 365) = 1.81 × 10<sup>8</sup> s **[1 mark]**

Determine the decay constant:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}$
- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{1.81\times10^{8}}$ = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Calculate the decay constant, in s^–1^, of radium-228.
Half-life of radium-228, t_1/2 = 5.75 years
Decay constant: λ = ln 2 / t_1/2 = ln 2 / (1.81 × 10^8) = 3.83 × 10^−9 s^−1

A sample is taken of the contaminated water. The activity of radium-228 in a sample of 1.0 kg of water is found to be 20 mBq.

The mass of water in 1.0 mol is 18 g.

Calculate

(i) the number of radium-228 atoms in 1.0 kg of the contaminated water

[2]

(ii) the ratio

`(number of molecules of water in 1.0 kg of water)/(number of Ra ^ 228 atoms in 1.0 kg of water)`

[2]
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Decay constant of radium-228, *λ* = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)
- Activity in 1.0 kg of water, *A* = 20 mBq = 0.020 Bq
- Avogadro's constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of water in 1.0 mol, *m* = 18 g = 0.018 kg

(i) The number of radium-228 atoms in 1.0 kg of the contaminated water is:

- Activity:  $A=λN$
- Number of atoms in 1.0 kg of water:  $N=\frac{A}{λ}=\frac{0.020}{3.83\times10^{-9}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Number of atoms in 1.0 kg of water:  N = 5.22 × 10<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) The ratio of molecules of water to the number of radium-228 atoms is:

- Number of water molecules in 1.0 kg = $\frac{N_{A}}{m}=\frac{6.02\times10^{23}}{0.018}$ = 3.34 × 10<sup>25</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Ratio = `(number of molecules of water in 1.0 kg of water)/(number of Ra ^ 228 atoms in 1.0 kg of water)`
- Ratio = $\frac{3.34\times10^{25}}{5.22\times10^{6}}$ = 6.4 × 10<sup>18</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Calculate the decay constant, in s^–1^, of radium-228. Decay constant: λ = ln2/(1.81 × 10^8) = 3.83 × 10^−9 s^−1

The activity of radium-228 in a sample of 1.0 kg of water is found to be 20 mBq.

The maximum safe limit for the activity of radium-228 in water has been set as 18.5 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the time, in days, for the activity of the contaminated water to be reduced to the safe limit.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the time for the activity to be reduced to the safe limit:

List the known quantities:

- Target activity, *A* = 18.5 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Initial activity, *A*<sub>*0*</sub> = 20 mBq kg<sup>−1</sup>
- Decay constant of radium-228, *λ* = 3.83 × 10<sup>−9</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)

Use the exponential decay equation for activity to determine the time:

- Exponential decay:  $A=A_{0}e^{-λt}$ **[1 mark]**
- `A / A _ 0 = e ^ - lambda t <-> ln ( A / A _ 0 ) = - lambda t <-> t = - (ln ( A / A _ 0 ))/(lambda)`
- Time (in s):  $t = - \frac{\ln ( \frac{18.5}{20} )}{3.83 \times 10^{- 9}}$ = 2.04 × 10<sup>7</sup> s **[1 mark]**
- Time (in days):  $t=\frac{2.04\times10^{7}}{60\times60\times24}$ = 236 days **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Define half−life.
parts.solution_md:
The definition of half−life is:

- The time taken for the number of nuclei / the activity (of the source); **[1 mark]**
- To decay / reduce by half; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The time it takes for the activity of the sample to decrease from 100% to 50% is the half-life. It is the same length of time as it would take to decrease from 50% activity to 25% activity. The half-life is constant for a particular isotope.*

> *The diagram shows how the activity of a radioactive sample changes over time. Each time the original activity halves, another half-life has passed.*

parts.problem_md:
Radioactive decay is often described as a spontaneous and random process.

State what is meant by

(i) radioactive decay

[2]

(ii) a spontaneous process

[2]

(iii) a random process

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Radioactive decay is defined as:

- The emission of a radioactive particle (alpha, beta or gamma); **[1 mark]**
- From a <u>nucleus</u>; **[1 mark]**

(ii) A spontaneous process is defined as:

- A decay which is unaffected by environmental changes; **[1 mark]**
- Such as temperature / pressure / chemical conditions; **[1 mark]**

(iii) A random process is defined as:

- The constant probability that a nucleus will decay (per unit time); **[1 mark]**
- (Because) it cannot be predicted which particular nucleus will decay next; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows the count rate of a radioactive substance measured by a Geiger-Müller tube.

![7-1-q2d-question-sl-sq-easy-phy](assets/007-7-1-q2d-question-sl-sq-easy-phy.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the feature of Fig. 1.1 which provides evidence for

(i) the random nature of radioactive decay

[1]

(ii) the spontaneous nature of radioactive decay

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The graph demonstrates the random nature of radioactive decay because:

- There are fluctuations in the curve **OR** the curve is not smooth; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The graph demonstrates the spontaneous nature of radioactive decay because:

- The decay curve is the same regardless of external conditions; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is not possible to determine exactly when radioactive nuclei will decay. It could be in the next minute, or it might not be for another 10 000 years or more!*

> *All we can do is look at the general **pattern** across a large number of radioactive nuclei which provides us with the half−life. The decay of an individual nucleus is **not** dependent on the others in the sample.*

> *The fluctuations in count rate, as shown on the graph, indicate that sometimes slightly more nuclei will decay in a period of time and sometimes slightly fewer!*

parts.problem_md:
The element neptunium has at least 24 isotopes. One of the isotopes is neptunium-231 $( Np_{93}^{231} )$, which has a half-life of 49 minutes.

(i) State what is meant by *isotopes* and circle the possible isotopes of neptunium

| `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 239` | `Np presubscript 94 presuperscript 231` | `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 219` | `Np presubscript 90 presuperscript 231` | `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 244` |
|---|---|---|---|---|

[3]

(ii) Define *half-life* and circle the correct expression for calculating the probability per second of decay of a nucleus of neptunium-231.

| $\frac{49}{0.693}$ | $\frac{0.693}{49}$ | $\frac{0.693}{49\times60}$ | $\frac{49\times60}{0.693}$ |
|---|---|---|---|

[3]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Isotopes of an element are:

- Nuclei which have the same proton number / atomic number / number of protons; **[1 mark]**
- But a different neutron number / number of neutrons; **[1 mark]**

Possible isotopes of neptunium:

- `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 239`, `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 219`, `Np presubscript 93 presuperscript 244` (all three circled); **[1 mark]**

(ii) Half-life is defined as:

- The time it takes for the initial activity (of a source) / number of nuclei (in a source); **[1 mark]**
- To reduce to one-half of its initial value; **[1 mark]**

The correct expression is:

- $( \\lambda = ) \frac{0.693}{49 \times 60}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *For part (i), make sure to look carefully at each option - the two incorrect options *`Np presubscript 94 presuperscript 231`* and *`Np presubscript 90 presuperscript 231`* have atomic (proton) numbers of 94 and 90 which means they would be completely **different elements*

> *For part (ii), you needed to realise that the probability per second of decay of a nucleus is the definition of **decay constant **and that you need to multiply the **half-life by 60** to convert it into seconds*

parts.problem_md:
Rubidium (Rb) was found in samples of moon rock which were retrieved from the Apollo missions. The isotope `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b` is known to have a half-life of 4.90 × 10<sup>10</sup>years.

One of the moon rock samples contains 1.2 mg of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`.

Show that the mass of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b` that the rock sample contained when the moon was formed 4.47 ×10<sup>9 </sup>years ago was about 1.3 mg.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Half-life of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$= 4.90 × 10<sup>10 </sup>years
- Current mass of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`, *m* = 1.2 mg = 1.2 × 10<sup>–3 </sup>g
- Time since the formation of the moon, *t* = 4.47 × 10<sup>9</sup> years** **

Calculate the decay constant  of the rubidium using the expression from the formula page:

- $λ=\frac{0.693}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}=\frac{0.693}{4.90\times10^{10}}$ = 1.41 × 10<sup>–11 </sup>year<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark] **

Use the decay equation from the formula page to calculate the mass *m* of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b` present in the rock sample 4.47 × 10<sup>9 </sup>years ago:

- $x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$ so *m* =$m_{0}e^{-λt}$ (because mass *m* is proportional to number of nuclei $x$)
- (1.20 × 10<sup>–3</sup>) = $m_{0} e^{- ( 1.41 \times 10^{-11} } ) \times ( 4.47 \times 10^{9 )}$ = 0.939 ×$m_{0}$
- $m_{0}$*= *$\frac{1.2\times10^{-3}}{0.939}$*=* 1.28 × 10<sup>–3</sup> g ~ 1.3 mg **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *All quantities such as number of radioactive nuclei, activity and mass of radioactive material decay exponentially and follow the equation *$x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$*. This is given on your formula page in your exam, but you must understand the quantities that **x** can represent.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Rubidium (Rb) was found in samples of moon rock which were retrieved from the Apollo missions. The isotope Rb-87 is known to have a half-life of 4.90 × 10^10 years. One of the moon rock samples contains 1.2 mg of Rb-87.

Decay constant of Rb-87, λ = 0.693/t½ = 0.693/(4.90 × 10^10) = 1.41 × 10^–11 year^–1

Calculate the activity of 1.2 mg of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`, *m* = 1.2 mg = 1.2 × 10<sup>–6</sup> kg
- Decay constant of `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b`, $λ$= 1.41 × 10<sup>–11</sup>year<sup>–1</sup> (from part a)

From data page:

- Unified atomic mass unit, *u* = 1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg

Calculate the number of nuclei, *N* , in 1.2 mg of  `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b` :

- $N=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{nucleus}}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{87u}$
- *N* =$\frac{1.2 \times 10^{- 6} }{87 \times ( 1.66 \times 10^{- 27} )}$ = 8.3 × 10<sup>18 </sup>**[1 mark]**** **

Calculate the decay constant in seconds:

- $λ$=  $\frac{1.41\times10^{-11}}{365\times24\times60\times60}$ = 4.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup> s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**** **

Calculate the activity of  `R presubscript 37 presuperscript 87 b` using the decay constant and the number of nuclei:

- *A* = *λN*
- *A *= (4.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) × (8.3 × 10<sup>18</sup>) = 3.7 Bq **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Though this question asks you to calculate the activity, you need to spot the tricky unit conversions throughout the question to gain full credit:*

- *For the first mark, calculating the number of nuclei using the atomic mass unit requires the mass of the sample to be converted to kilograms (watch out too for the mass number 87, which means there are 87 nucleons in rubidium each contributing a unified atomic mass unit)*
- *If you are ever in doubt regarding a unit conversion, think 'should this value get larger or smaller?' –  there will be fewer decays per second than per year so the decay constant should decrease in size when converting from per year to per second*

parts.problem_md:
Radioactive carbon dating is a method for determining the age of samples containing organic material. This is a commonly used method for terrestrial objects.

Pieces of ancient wood found in a fireplace at an archaeological site can be dated by measuring the activity of carbon-14. A sample contains one carbon-14 atom per 8.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> carbon-12 atoms. In living wood, the concentration of carbon-14 atoms is greater at one carbon-14 atom per 3.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> carbon-12 atoms.

The half-life of carbon-14 is 1.8 × 10<sup>11</sup> s.

Explain why the concentration of carbon-14 is greater in living wood and calculate the age, in years, of the sample taken from the archaeological site.
parts.solution_md:
Explain why the concentration of carbon-14 is greater in living wood:

- Carbon-14 is constantly absorbed / replaced in living wood; **[1 mark]**
- (In dead wood, it is not replaced, but) carbon-14 undergoes radioactive decay over time **AND** carbon-12 is <u>stable</u>; **[1 mark]**

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of carbon-14, $t_{\frac{1}{2}}$= 1.8 × 10<sup>11</sup> s
- Initial ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 (in living wood) = 1/(3 × 10<sup>10</sup>)
- Final ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 (in the ancient wood) = 1/(8 × 10<sup>10</sup>)

Calculate the decay constant of carbon-14:

- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{1.8\times10^{11}}$ = 3.9 × 10<sup>–12</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the elapsed time using the decay equation:

- $x=x_{0}e^{-λt}$ where $x$  represents the ratio of C-14
- $\frac{1}{8 \times 10^{10} = \frac{1}{3 \times 10^{10} e^{-(} \text{parentheses} 3.9 \times 10^{-12} } ) t}$ **[1 mark]**
- Multiply both sides by 3 × 10<sup>10</sup> to obtain 0.375 = $e^{- ( 3.9 \times 10^{- 12} ) t}$
- ln 0.375 = – (3.9 × 10<sup>–12</sup>) × t
- t = 2.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> s = 7900 years **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
A student sets up a radioactive source and a Geiger counter to investigate how the count rate of the source varies with time.

State and explain how the student could demonstrate

(i) the spontaneous nature of radioactive decay,

[2]

(ii) the random nature of radioactive decay.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i)** **The student could demonstrate the spontaneous nature of radioactive decay by:

- Repeating the experiment in different (environmental) conditions e.g. temperature, pressure, humidity, chemicals; **[1 mark]**
- To show that the rate of decay / activity does not change; **[1 mark]**

**OR**** max ****one mark ****for:**

- (Spontaneous decay means) the rate of decay / activity (of a nucleus) is not affected by environmental / external factors; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The student could demonstrate the random nature of radioactive decay by:

- Plotting a graph of count rate against time (using a data logger / computer software); **[1 mark]**
- To show the presence of fluctuations **OR** that the (decay) curve is not smooth; **[1 mark]**

**OR**** max ****one mark ****for:**

- (Random decay means) the time of decay (of a nucleus) cannot be predicted **OR** a nucleus has a constant probability (of decaying) in a given time; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You could also draw a diagram or example decay curve to help illustrate your answer:*

![spontaneous-random-decay-ma](assets/010-spontaneous-random-decay-ma.png)

Complete the equation for this decay.

`Tc _ 43 ^ 101 -> Ru _...... ^...... + beta _...... ^...... + ......`

parts.problem_md:
The radioisotope uranium-238 `( U _ 92 ^ 238 )` decays through a decay chain to the radioisotope lead-206 $( Pb_{82}^{206} )$, which is stable.

During the decay chain, 8 alpha particles are emitted, and X beta particles are emitted.

Calculate the value of X.
parts.solution_md:
Recall the proton and mass number of alpha and beta particles:

- An alpha particle has 2 protons and 4 neutrons / `alpha presubscript 2 presuperscript 4` **AND** A beta particle is an electron / `beta presubscript negative 1 end presubscript presuperscript 0` **[1 mark] **

Calculate the new proton and mass number after 8 alpha decays, labelling this unknown isotope as Y:

- 8 alpha decays means the proton number will decrease by 8 × 2 = 16 and the mass number will decrease by 8 × 4 = 32
- $U_{92}^{238} \rightarrow Y_{76}^{206} + 8 \\alpha pre_{2} pre^{4}$** [1 mark]**

Calculate the change in proton number from isotope Y to lead-206:

- `Y presubscript 76 presuperscript 206` to `P presubscript 82 presuperscript 206 b` means the proton number must increase by 6
- `Y _ 76 ^ 206 -> P _ 82 ^ 206 b + 6 beta _ - 1 ^ 0`** [1 mark]**
- This means 6 beta particles are emitted: X = 6 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks] **

> *Notice that tackling this question hinges on knowing the proton and mass number of an alpha particle and a beta particle, even though stating this wasn’t explicitly asked in the question. *

> *Knowing the basic properties of radioactive decay – e.g. type, nature, penetration depth, etc. – is really crucial and you should be on the lookout to apply them in different contexts.*

parts.problem_md:
The half-life of uranium-238 is so long in comparison to any of the isotopes in its decay chain that we can assume the number of lead-206 nuclei, $N_{Pb}$ at any time is equal to the number of uranium-238 that have decayed.

The number of uranium-238 nuclei $N_{U}$ at time *t* is given by the equation:

$N_{U}=N_{0}e^{-λt}$

where $N_{0}$ is the number of uranium-238 nuclei at *t = *0.

Show that the ratio $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}$ is given by:

$\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=e^{λt}-1$
parts.solution_md:
Write an expression for the initial number of uranium-238 nuclei:

- Initial number of uranium-238 nuclei = number of decayed nuclei + number of uranium-238 nuclei remaining
- $N_{0}=N_{Pb}+N_{U}$** ****[1 mark] **

Rearrange this expression for the number of lead-206 nuclei and divide both sides by $N_{U}$ to get an expression for the ratio required:

- $N_{Pb}=N_{0}-N_{U}$
- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{N_{0}}{N_{U}}-\frac{N_{U}}{N_{U}}$  **[1 mark]**

Substitute the expression for $N_{U}$ and simplify the expression:

- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{N_{0}}{N_{0}e^{-λt}}-1$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{N_{Pb}}{N_{U}}=\frac{1}{e^{-λt}}-1=e^{λt}-1$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Make sure you are comfortable interpreting the ‘exponential decay’ equation as the number of nuclei remaining in a sample. That way, you can always form an expression for the **initial number** of nuclei, in terms of a sum of the number of decayed nuclei and the number of nuclei remaining.*

parts.problem_md:
Enriched uranium fuel is a mixture of the fissionable uranium-235 with the more naturally abundant uranium-238. Mixtures of radioactive nuclides such as this are very common in the nuclear power industry.

Two samples of radioactive nuclides **X** and **Y** each have an activity of $A_{0}$ at *t* = 0. They are subsequently mixed together. The half-lives of **X **and **Y** are 16 and 8 years, respectively.

Show that the total activity of the mixture at time *t *= 48 years is equal to $\frac{9}{64}A_{0}$.
parts.solution_md:
Write an expression for the activity of each nuclide in terms of the number of half-lives completed:

- $A_{X} = A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{N}$  and $A_{Y} = A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{N}$ where *N* is the number of half-lives
- The amount of time elapsed, *t, *can be written as some multiple *N * of half-lives: $t=N\timest_{1/2}$

- Number of half-lives:* *$N=\frac{t}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}$ **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the activity of each nuclide in terms of the time elapsed:

- $A_{X} = A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{ \frac{48}{16} }$ **AND** $A_{Y} = A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{ \frac{48}{8} }$ **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the total activity *A  *of the mixture:

- $A=A_{X}+A_{Y}$
- $A = A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{ \frac{48}{16} } + A_{0} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{ \frac{48}{8} }$

Simplify the expression fully:

- $A = A_{0} [ ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{3} + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} )^{6} ]$`= \left(\frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{64}\right) = \frac{9}{64} A_{0}` **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You may have simply determined the number of half-lives of each isotope in 48 years by dividing 48 years by 8 and then 16, and halving each **A*<sub>*0 *</sub>*the appropriate number of times before combining. This method is equally correct, but you must clearly show and explain your reasoning with each step.*

parts.problem_md:
A pure sample of polonium-213 is produced in a research laboratory.

The half-life of `Po presubscript 84 presuperscript 213` is very small compared with the half-life of `Pb presubscript 82 presuperscript 209`. After a very short time, the ionising radiation detected from the sample is mainly from the beta-minus decay of the lead-209 nuclei.

The half-life of `Pb presubscript 82 presuperscript 209` is 3.3 hours.

(i) State what is meant by the *decay constant *of a radioactive isotope.

[2]

(ii) Calculate the decay constant, in s<sup>−1</sup>, of lead-209.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Decay constant is defined as:

**EITHER**

- The probability of decay (of a nucleus) / the fraction of the number of nuclei in a sample that decay; **[1 mark]**
- Per unit time; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- $\\lambda = - ( \frac{d N}{d t} ) \frac{1}{N}$; **[1 mark]**
- Where $- ( \frac{d N}{d t} )$ is the rate of decay of nuclei and *N* is the number of nuclei in the sample; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the decay constant of lead-209:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of lead-209, *t*<sub>1/2</sub> = 3.3 hours = 3.3 × 60 × 60 = 11 880 s **[1 mark]**

Calculate the decay constant, *λ*:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$
- $λ=\frac{0.693}{11880}$ **[1 mark]**
- $λ=5.83\times10^{-5}=5.8\times10^{-5}s^{-1}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**
